item.title: Dynamic Workflows in Claude Code
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Anthropic has introduced dynamic workflows in Claude Code, a research-preview feature for the tasks too big for a single pass — work you’d normally plan in quarters, done in days. What the announcement describes:

  • What it is. Claude writes an orchestration script that breaks a task into subtasks and fans them out across tens to hundreds of subagents running in parallel within one session, checking each result before folding it in and returning a single coordinated answer.
  • How it converges. Agents attack the problem from independent angles while other agents try to refute what they find, and the run keeps iterating until the answers agree. That redundancy-plus-refutation loop is, per the post, how a workflow “reaches results a single pass can’t.”
  • What it’s for. Codebase-wide bug hunts, profiler-guided optimization and security audits, and hardening passes (auth checks, input validation, unsafe patterns); large migrations and language ports spanning thousands of files; and high-stakes work you want checked twice, with adversarial agents trying to break the result before you see it.
  • Long-running and resumable. It is built for jobs that run for hours or days. Progress is saved as the run goes, so an interrupted job resumes instead of restarting, and because the coordination lives outside the conversation the plan holds its shape as the task grows.
  • Where it runs. Research preview in the Claude Code CLI, desktop app, and VS Code extension on Max, Team, and Enterprise (admin-enabled) plans, plus the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.
  • How to start. Ask Claude to “create a workflow,” or turn on the new ultracode setting (the effort menu’s maximum, xhigh), which lets Claude decide for itself when a task warrants one. It is on by default on Max, Team, and the API, and off by default on Enterprise at launch. Anthropic warns it consumes substantially more tokens than a normal session, so the first run pauses for confirmation and admins can disable it.

Case study: rewriting Bun

The announcement’s marquee example is the rewrite of Bun, the JavaScript runtime. Jarred Sumner used dynamic workflows to port it from Zig to Rust: roughly 750,000 lines of Rust, 99.8% of the existing test suite passing, eleven days from first commit to merge. One workflow mapped the right Rust lifetime for every struct field in the Zig code; the next wrote each .rs file as a behavior-identical port of its .zig counterpart, hundreds of agents in parallel with two reviewers on each file; a fix loop then drove the build and test suite until both ran clean; and an overnight workflow opened a separate PR for each unnecessary data copy it found. The post notes the result is not yet in production, so the 99.8% is a test-pass rate on a port rather than a measure of shipped software running under load.

My Notes

  • The script makes the run inspectable. Claude writes the coordination as an explicit script instead of burying it in one long completion. So you can read the plan, the subtasks, and what each subagent was told. When a long run goes wrong, you can find the step that broke it, and you can approve or fix the plan before hundreds of agents act on it. That matters more as runs get longer and costlier to redo.

  • Convergence is not correctness. The run stops when the agents and their refuters agree, and that agreement is reported as a verified result. But they are the same base model reading the same context, so they share blind spots: wrong answers can converge as cleanly as right ones. The claim only holds if the refuters are genuinely adversarial, not just agreeable, and that is the part still to be proven.

  • Dynamic authoring replaces topology search. Earlier multi-agent work searched for good agent topologies offline (ADAS, AFlow, and MASS, which found topology matters least, behind the prompts at both ends). Dynamic workflows have Claude write the orchestration fresh for each task. That swaps an expensive offline search for per-task generation, but the risk moves rather than vanishes: whether a generated plan beats a tuned fixed one, when a bad plan costs hours of parallel compute, is the open question.

  • It is the Ralph loop, grown up. The cheapest version of this idea is the Ralph loop: one agent in a while true shell loop, fed the same prompt until the repo looks done, with git as the only memory. Dynamic workflows keep that deterministic outer loop but let Claude write it, fan the work across parallel agents, and add agents whose job is to attack the results. The Ralph loop trusts repetition to converge; this trusts refutation. What is unproven is whether the extra machinery, and the much larger token bill, earns its keep on tasks a plain loop would have finished anyway.

item.title: Claude Code Beyond the Prompt
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Arpan Patel wrote a long field guide to running Claude Code as a programmable agent instead of a terminal chatbot: the .claude directory, CLAUDE.md the way Boris Cherny writes it, skills, custom subagents, plugins, the underused commands, MCPs, and the workflow habits the Anthropic team actually runs. The author’s badge says it hit #7 on the Hacker News front page.

What the Guide Covers

The operating principle. Run Claude Code as an agent that needs guardrails, not a prompt-and-wait chatbot.

  • Give Claude a way to verify its own work, whether a test, a build, or a grep-able condition, so it keeps iterating until the code runs. Cherny pegs this single move at a 2-3x quality bump.
  • Drop into read-only plan mode before any change that touches more than one file, so you can review and edit the plan before it turns into code. Skip it for small fixes.
  • Reference files with @path and pipe errors in with cat error.log | claude, because exact context beats an approximate description.
  • Write a crisp brief and let Claude run rather than steering it line by line, since the model does better when you delegate than when you pair-program.

The .claude directory. A layered config system, not just a home for CLAUDE.md.

  • Split config by scope: project files (.claude/, committed) describe the project, global files (~/.claude/) describe you.
  • Let CLAUDE.md files cascade in a monorepo, so a service folder adds local conventions on top of the root file.
  • Move folder-specific guidance into path-gated rules/*.md, so it loads only where it applies instead of bloating every session.
  • Prefer skills over loose commands/*.md, since skills carry supporting files, tool restrictions, and agent overrides.

CLAUDE.md. The file Claude reads at the start of every session, kept as a guardrail rather than a knowledge base.

  • Keep it short by cutting any line whose removal wouldn’t cause a mistake, because long files bury the rules that matter.
  • After each mistake, tell Claude to “update CLAUDE.md so you don’t repeat this,” so the file becomes a curated gotcha list in the model’s own phrasing.
  • Limit it to build commands, run order, single-test invocations, and a Gotchas section of real shipped bugs, and leave out style conventions and codebase tours that go stale.
  • Commit rules straight from PR-review comments with @claude, so every review becomes a permanent fix (Cherny’s “Compounding Engineering”).

CLAUDE.local.md. A gitignored sibling that loads like CLAUDE.md but never leaves your machine.

  • Paste recurring PR-review feedback into it as you read it, so it becomes a private rule file tuned to the comments you keep getting.
  • Keep project feedback and personal habits in separate sections, and prune once something is muscle memory, so the file stays easy to maintain.

Skills. Folders that package reusable expertise as slash commands.

  • Put a SKILL.md in a folder; the folder name becomes the command, so a repeated workflow turns into something you invoke by name.
  • Rely on progressive disclosure: only the ~100-token description loads at session start and the full instructions load when the skill fires, which keeps context lean.
  • Use frontmatter to restrict tools, pin an agent, or require explicit invocation for skills with side effects, so a deploy skill runs only when you type it.
  • Heuristic: if you’ve typed the same instructions twice, write a skill.

Subagents. Separate Claude instances with their own context and scoped tools.

  • Hand a fifty-file investigation to a subagent, so it doesn’t crowd the main session’s context.
  • Keep a reviewer agent read-only, because a reviewer that can patch starts defending its own fixes instead of flagging them.
  • Give a review agent a “Do NOT flag” section, so its output isn’t drowned in nitpicks.
  • Add isolation: worktree to run one agent per task across parallel git worktrees.

Plugins. Installable bundles of skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers.

  • Install through /plugin, so a team’s setup travels instead of staying on one machine.
  • Start with /code-review (parallel agents, confidence-scored findings) and /feature-dev.
  • Add a language server plugin for symbol-level navigation and on-edit diagnostics, which the team rates the highest-impact install.

Underused commands. What’s past /clear and /compact.

  • Use /rewind to roll back to a checkpoint instead of typing “that didn’t work,” which only buries the bad attempt in context.
  • Reach for /branch, /batch, /voice, and /insights to fork a session, fan work out, dictate prompts, and review your usage monthly.
  • Set /goal to a verifiable completion condition and let Claude grind until it holds.
  • Force compaction before 300-400k tokens, where context rot starts on the 1M-token model.
  • For mass edits, generate the task list, hand-check three, tighten the prompt, then loop. That is how he migrated roughly 2,000 component files.

MCPs. A protocol for reaching external systems from inside the session.

  • Wire in servers like GitHub, Postgres, Sentry, Figma, or Linear through MCP (Model Context Protocol), so the agent reasons about your whole stack, not just the repo.
  • Install few: every server enlarges the tool list Claude reasons over, and a bloated list degrades decision quality.
  • Treat an Obsidian vault as three memory tiers: a daily session log (hot), project notes Claude rehydrates at session start (warm), and promoted decisions and reusable notes (cold).

Daily workflow and team habits. How the Anthropic team runs it day to day.

  • Reproduce a bug with a failing test before asking for a fix, so the fix isn’t a guess.
  • Run three to five parallel sessions in separate git worktrees, the habit the team rates the single biggest unlock.
  • Pair a writer session with a fresh reviewer session, so the review carries no implementation bias.
  • Default to Opus at high effort, since a weaker model that needs correcting is slower overall.
  • Never let Claude claim success without evidence, because the trust-then-verify gap is the biggest source of bad output.

My Notes

  • Harness over model. The guide’s bigger point is the same one Anthropic makes in its official large-codebases piece: what you build around the model matters more than which model you run.

  • /goal, a built-in Ralph loop. It packages the pattern, retry until an external check passes, as a single command.

item.title: Use Boring Languages with LLMs
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Jacob Young argues that coding agents produce more reliable output in languages and ecosystems with low variance in their training data, and that Go is the best mainstream language for this moment because its conventions, standard library, and one-right-way tooling give an agent fewer ways to go wrong.

What the article argues

The case, in the order the article makes it:

  • The core claim: coding agents inherit the variance of their training data. Ecosystems with heavy fragmentation produce the worst agentic output, and the ones with the strongest conventions produce the best.
  • Inference is a gamble: even when code is cheap, any single generation might install a needless package or reproduce an outdated pattern. The bet is to spend tokens where the model’s weights are most reinforced, which yields median output, and the median program is mostly doing the basics anyway: reading files, serving requests, responding over the network.
  • JavaScript and Python are the cautionary cases: the 2024 State of JS survey describes a fragmented ecosystem, and Python forces a matrix of choices among pip, Poetry, and uv, sync versus async, Django versus FastAPI. The public corpus reflects every variant in roughly equal weight, so the model has no single idiom to default to.
  • Ruby on Rails and Go are the counter-cases: Ruby on Rails produces more consistent agentic output because there is essentially one Rails, where JavaScript has a dozen production-grade frameworks covering the same features. Convention over configuration, once a win for human programmers, now helps machines more.
  • Go gives an agent five specific advantages:
    • Goroutines avoid the colored-function problem: there is no async-versus-sync split for the model to track.
    • The standard library carries a large share of real services, net/http and the Google-funded cryptography packages in particular, without reaching for third-party code.
    • One-right-way tooling (gofmt, go vet, gopls, golangci-lint) enforces a single canonical style and feeds the agent real-time semantic and lint feedback.
    • Garbage collection gives native-like performance without asking the agent to manage memory, which the article contrasts with Rust’s borrow checker (“a constant fight for agents”) and the memory bugs that fill C and C++ training data.
    • The set of footguns is small and bounded, unlike Python with arbitrary metaclasses.
  • What the article concludes: not that Go is the best language, but that this language and toolchain can write the majority of non-visual software, the next CLI, backend server, or agent orchestrator.

My Notes

The notes below weigh the thesis from both sides, each marked for or against.

  • Variance may be the wrong variable. Against the thesis. The article credits low corpus variance but never accounts for corpus size, a separate variable. JavaScript and Python are the most fragmented mainstream ecosystems, yet also the most-represented in training data, and code models are strongest on well-represented languages and weaker on low-resource ones like OCaml or Racket [1]. The strongest real-task evidence agrees: on Multi-SWE-bench [3], which extends SWE-bench’s Python tasks to seven more languages (Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C, C++), models resolve Python issues at by far the highest rate of the eight, even though Python is one of the most fragmented ecosystems. The authors caution that the agent harnesses were themselves tuned on Python, so part of that lead is tooling rather than training data.

  • The toolchain advantage isn’t about the language alone. Against the thesis, on its internal logic. The article names two ingredients for good agentic output: a consistent training corpus and “one-right-way tooling for testing and feedback at runtime.” The second is language-independent: deterministic in-loop tooling (gofmt, go vet, gopls, golangci-lint) is a checkable signal the agent can iterate against, and any ecosystem with a strong checker provides one no matter how consistent its corpus is. So only the corpus half supports picking a boring language. The tooling half holds for any language with good tools.

  • Betting on the median optimizes the cheap part. Against the thesis, on its payoff. The basics the article’s wager targets are also where a competent engineer was already fast, and where an agent’s leverage is smallest. The work that actually costs human time is the non-median part: the unfamiliar API, the awkward edge case, the migration nobody has done before. ProgramBench shows that gap with numbers: asked to rebuild whole programs from scratch with no constraint on language, nine frontier models fully resolve none of 200 tasks, and the failures are architectural rather than matters of language idiom. Picking a boring language makes the agent reliable exactly where reliability was cheapest to get.

  • The advantage shrinks as harnesses improve. Against the thesis, on its durability. The article cites Claude Code’s “hard-coded some bias for JavaScript frameworks” as proof fragmentation is costly. But that fix lives in the harness, not the language. As harness conventions (system-prompt defaults, convention files, pinned lockfiles) normalize a fragmented ecosystem, the reason to switch languages weakens. The advice is strongest today and weaker with every harness improvement.

  • The Hacker News thread (228 points, 168 comments) divides on the same fault lines. The salient points, by side.

    • Against the thesis:
      • The most common objection is corpus size rather than variance, the point in the first note above. Commenters report the model writes “much better PHP, than Swift” because there is far more open-source PHP to train on, and that the worst results come from GDScript, “python minus the huge corpus of training data.”
      • The available benchmarks don’t single Go out. A commenter cited AutoCodeBench [2], a 20-language Pass@1 benchmark, for models being “better at writing Elixir than most other languages,” but that benchmark classifies Elixir as low-resource and clusters its four popular languages (Python, C++, Java, C#) within a narrow band, roughly 50 to 54 Pass@1. Go is not in that popular set, and on Multi-SWE-bench’s real issue-resolution tasks [3] it ranks in the middle, ahead of JavaScript and TypeScript but behind Python and Java. No mainstream language stands out.
      • A large camp argues the property that helps is strictness rather than boringness, and would go the other way toward Rust, OCaml, or Haskell: required Result/Option handling means “if it compiles, chances are higher the code is correct,” which catches more agent errors than a low-variance corpus does.
      • Goroutines drew specific pushback. Several report agents “trip up a lot on the races and locking” in Go and have moved their agent work to Rust, and note the article gives no evidence for the goroutine claim.
      • Others argue human familiarity matters more than the model’s preference, since “the bottleneck isn’t what languages the LLM can handle, but what I can handle” coming out of it.
    • For the thesis:
      • The feedback-loop point drew the most agreement: compile-time errors and clear compiler messages let the agent iterate, which commenters found true in Elm and Rust as much as in Go.
      • Anecdotal wins for Go: one reports the code Sonnet “produces for Go is much better than the Python it creates,” another that LLM-assisted Node-to-Go ports came out clean and cut memory roughly tenfold.
      • “Pit of success” was offered as the better name for the real effect: predictable defaults that are hard to get wrong.

References

  1. Cassano, Federico, Gouwar, John, Lucchetti, Francesca, Schlesinger, Claire, Freeman, Anders, Anderson, Carolyn Jane, Feldman, Molly Q., Greenberg, Michael, Jangda, Abhinav, Guha, Arjun. “Knowledge Transfer from High-Resource to Low-Resource Programming Languages for Code LLMs.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2308.09895), August 19, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.09895
  2. Chou, Jason, Liu, Ao, Deng, Yuchi, Zeng, Zhiying, Zhang, Tao, Zhu, Haotian, Cai, Jianwei, Mao, Yue, Zhang, Chenchen, Tan, Lingyun, Xu, Ziyan, Zhai, Bohui, Liu, Hengyi, Zhu, Speed, Zhou, Wiggin, Lian, Fengzong. “AutoCodeBench: Large Language Models are Automatic Code Benchmark Generators.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2508.09101), August 12, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09101
  3. Zan, Daoguang, Huang, Zhirong, Liu, Wei, Chen, Hanwu, Zhang, Linhao, Xin, Shulin, Chen, Lu, Liu, Qi, Zhong, Xiaojian, Li, Aoyan, Liu, Siyao, Xiao, Yongsheng, Chen, Liangqiang, Zhang, Yuyu, Su, Jing, Liu, Tianyu, Long, Rui, Shen, Kai, Xiang, Liang. “Multi-SWE-bench: A Multilingual Benchmark for Issue Resolving.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.02605), April 3, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02605

item.title: AutoCodeBench: Large Language Models are Automatic Code Benchmark Generators
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In AutoCodeBench: Large Language Models are Automatic Code Benchmark Generators [1], Chou et al. (Tencent) introduce AutoCodeGen, an automated pipeline that turns existing code snippets into a 3,920-problem benchmark spanning 20 programming languages — and find that even the strongest LLMs top out below 53% Pass@1.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, with code generation emerging as a key area of focus. While numerous benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate their code generation abilities, these benchmarks face several critical limitations. First, they often rely on manual annotations, which are time-consuming and difficult to scale across different programming languages and problem complexities. Second, most existing benchmarks focus primarily on Python, while the few multilingual benchmarks suffer from limited difficulty and uneven language distribution. To address these challenges, we propose AutoCodeGen, an automated method for generating high-difficulty multilingual code generation datasets without manual annotations. AutoCodeGen ensures the correctness and completeness of test cases by generating test inputs with LLMs and obtaining test outputs through a multilingual sandbox, while achieving high data quality through reverse-order problem generation and multiple filtering steps. Using this novel method, we introduce AutoCodeBench, a large-scale code generation benchmark comprising 3,920 problems evenly distributed across 20 programming languages. It is specifically designed to evaluate LLMs on challenging, diverse, and practical multilingual tasks. We evaluate over 30 leading open-source and proprietary LLMs on AutoCodeBench and its simplified version AutoCodeBench-Lite. The results show that even the most advanced LLMs struggle with the complexity, diversity, and multilingual nature of these tasks. Besides, we introduce AutoCodeBench-Complete, specifically designed for base models to assess their few-shot code generation capabilities. We hope the AutoCodeBench series will serve as a valuable resource and inspire the community to focus on more challenging and practical multilingual code generation scenarios.

Method

The core trick in AutoCodeGen is that it builds each problem backwards. Conventional benchmarks start from a hand-written problem statement and then attach a reference solution and tests; AutoCodeGen starts from working code and only writes the problem last, so every item ships with a verified solution and executable tests by construction. The pipeline runs in four stages over an LLM and a multilingual sandbox:

  • Solution and test inputs. Seeded with real multilingual code snippets, an LLM writes a code solution plus public and private test-input functions for it.
  • Ground-truth outputs. The solution and test inputs are concatenated and run in a multilingual sandbox; the captured outputs are assembled by the LLM into complete, executable test functions.
  • Reverse-order problem generation. Only now — given a working solution and its tests — does the LLM write the natural-language programming problem, which guarantees the problem is solvable and checkable.
  • Three-stage filtering. Multiple sampling drops problems that are too easy; an LLM-as-Critic discards low-quality items; and diversity-based tagging balances the distribution across task categories.

The result is AutoCodeBench: 3,920 problems evenly spread over 20 languages (Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Go, Shell, C#, Dart, Elixir, Julia, Kotlin, Perl, PHP, Racket, R, Ruby, Rust, Scala, Swift, TypeScript), with over 60% rated hard, averaging 498 characters and 9.6 test cases per problem, and spanning 14 practical task categories. Two derivatives accompany it: AutoCodeBench-Lite, roughly 1,500 of the hardest problems (those solved at least twice but by few models) selected to amplify model differences, and AutoCodeBench-Complete, a few-shot completion variant aimed at base models.

One design choice runs through every stage: each LLM role — solution writer, test assembler, problem author, and quality critic — is filled by a DeepSeek-series model. Because models used as generators or judges tend to recognize and reward outputs in their own style [2], mixing families into the construction would hand a quiet home-field advantage to whichever families helped build the benchmark. Confining the loop to one family keeps that bias from tilting the comparison toward any of the other 30-plus models under evaluation — though, as the authors acknowledge, it cannot rule out a residual tilt toward what DeepSeek itself finds natural to write and to accept.

Results

The authors evaluate more than 30 models — open-source checkpoints from 1.5B to 1T parameters plus leading proprietary systems (OpenAI o3/o4-mini/GPT-4.1, Claude Opus 4 and Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-R1/V3, the Qwen and Qwen-Coder series, GLM-4.5, Kimi-K2, and others) — using Pass@1 as the metric. Beyond the aggregate score, they split languages into four popular (Python, C++, Java, C#) and four low-resource (Racket, Shell, Elixir, TS) sets by TIOBE rank, isolate a 1,622-problem multi-logic subset (problems requiring several coordinated functions or classes, identified with DeepSeek-V3), and run a six-language manual audit with six professional annotators.

The headline is a low ceiling and a wide field:

  • No model clears 53 average Pass@1 on AutoCodeBench. Claude Opus 4 ranks first in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes; the benchmark is hard enough that the whole field clusters below the bar.
  • The combined upper bound reaches 74.8 — far above any single model — so models are complementary rather than uniformly strong, and no single system dominates across languages.
  • AutoCodeBench-Lite widens the gaps, yet the best model still reaches only 64.5 Pass@1 on it.
  • Popular languages barely separate models (50.4–53.8), while low-resource languages spread them wide (45.3–62.0), with Claude Opus 4 leading by a clear margin — evidence that low-resource languages get short-changed in most models’ training.
  • Niche languages top the per-language ranking. On Table 4’s per-language upper bound [1] — the share of each language’s problems solved by at least one of the 30+ models — Elixir (97.5), Kotlin (89.5), C# (88.4), and Racket (88.3) lead, while the mainstream languages trail: Python 63.3, JavaScript 59.2, TypeScript 61.3, Go 69.1, PHP 52.8 (Java at 78.7 and C++ at 74.7 fall in between). The paper attributes the inversion to its difficulty filter: the easy-problem remover (DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite) is strongest on popular languages, so it stripped proportionally more of their easy problems and left the survivors harder. These per-language numbers feature in the debate over whether to favor low-variance “boring” languages for coding agents, covered in Use Boring Languages with LLMs.
  • Multi-logic problems hurt everyone. Every model drops on the multi-logic subset; Claude Opus 4 declines least, while several frontier models fall hardest.
  • The benchmark itself audits clean: across six languages, annotators judged 87.6% of items valid, well above the models’ own 66.9 upper bound and 44.6 Claude-Opus-4 score on the same slice.

My Notes

  • Synthesis over translation — multilingual code benchmarks usually buy breadth one of two ways, and AutoCodeGen takes neither. MultiPL-E [3] machine-translates Python problems like HumanEval into other languages, which inherits Python-shaped structure and can yield unidiomatic targets; McEval [4] hand-annotates 40 languages natively, which is faithful but bounded by what human annotators can label. Generating problems directly from native target-language code is the third path: it keeps per-language idiom while shedding the annotation cost, which is what lets the benchmark span 20 languages at 60%+ hard difficulty without a large labeling team.
  • Contamination, attacked from the other side — the central threat to any code benchmark is leakage of test problems into training data. LiveCodeBench [5] fights this temporally, harvesting fresh contest problems published after a model’s training cutoff. AutoCodeGen fights it generatively, synthesizing problems that never existed publicly. The trade is real but unresolved: a synthesized problem has no public origin to leak, yet it is still drawn from the distribution of code the generator was trained on, so distributional contamination remains an open question for synthetic benchmarks rather than a solved one.
  • Multi-function tasks below repo scale — single-function benchmarks (HumanEval-style) and repo-level agentic ones like SWE-bench [6] and ProgramBench bracket a middle ground: tasks that need several coordinated functions but no repository to navigate. The 1,622-problem multi-logic subset targets that middle ground, and the across-the-board drop on it [1] is a concrete sign that single-function fluency overstates how ready these models are for the multi-component work real coding agents actually do.

References

  1. Chou, Jason, Ao Liu, Yuchi Deng, Zhiying Zeng, Tao Zhang, Haotian Zhu, Jianwei Cai, Yue Mao, Chenchen Zhang, Lingyun Tan, Ziyan Xu, Bohui Zhai, Hengyi Liu, Speed Zhu, Wiggin Zhou, and Fengzong Lian (Hunyuan Team, Tencent). “AutoCodeBench: Large Language Models are Automatic Code Benchmark Generators.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2508.09101), August 12, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09101

  3. Cassano, Federico, John Gouwar, Daniel Nguyen, Sydney Nguyen, Luna Phipps-Costin, Donald Pinckney, Ming-Ho Yee, Yangtian Zi, Carolyn Jane Anderson, Molly Q. item.title: How Claude Code Works in Large Codebases: Best Practices and Where to Start
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Anthropic opens its Claude Code at scale series with the patterns it has seen across million-line monorepos, decades-old legacy systems, and orgs running Claude Code over dozens of microservices. The article argues the harness (CLAUDE.md files, hooks, skills, plugins, and MCP servers) does more for outcomes than the model swap, and prescribes an order in which to build it.

Summary of the Article

What “large” means. Multi-million-line monorepos, decades-old legacy systems, dozens of microservices across separate repos, organizations with thousands of developers, and codebases in C, C++, C#, Java, or PHP. The patterns generalize across all of these.

How Claude Code navigates. It traverses the file system, reads files, greps, and follows references on the developer’s machine. There is no embedding pipeline and no central index. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) tools fail at scale because the index falls behind active engineering teams and returns stale results without flagging them. Agentic search avoids that, but it needs enough starting context to know where to look.

The harness matters as much as the model. The ecosystem around the model, the harness, drives Claude Code performance more than the model alone. There are five extension points and two capabilities, and the build order matters because each layer depends on the previous one. The cover image above shows when each one is active across a session.

  1. CLAUDE.md. Context files Claude reads automatically every session. Root file for the big picture, subdirectory files for local conventions. Keep them lean: every byte loads every session.

  2. Hooks. Most teams use hooks to prevent mistakes. The more valuable use is continuous improvement. A stop-hook can propose CLAUDE.md updates while the session context is fresh. A start-hook can load team-specific context dynamically. Hooks also enforce lint and format more reliably than asking Claude to remember.

  3. Skills. Packaged expertise that loads on demand. A security-review skill loads when Claude is reviewing for vulnerabilities. A deployment skill scoped to a path doesn’t load elsewhere. This is how the harness scales without bloating CLAUDE.md.

  4. Plugins. A bundle of skills, hooks, and MCP configs in one installable package, distributed through marketplaces. Solves the problem of good setups staying tribal: new engineers get the team’s full context on day one.

  5. LSP (language server protocol). Symbol-level navigation: go-to-definition and find-all-references instead of text matching. Without it, grep on a common name returns thousands of hits and Claude burns context filtering them. Called out as one of the highest-value investments for multi-language codebases.

  6. MCP (model context protocol). How Claude reaches internal tools and data it can’t otherwise touch. Powerful but easy to overbuild. The article warns against starting here before the basics are working.

  7. Subagents. A separate Claude instance with its own context window. Common pattern: one subagent maps a subsystem and writes findings to a file, then the main agent edits with the full picture.

Three configuration patterns.

  • Make the codebase navigable. Keep CLAUDE.md lean and layered. Initialize Claude in subdirectories rather than the repo root, since it walks up the tree automatically. Scope test and lint commands per subdirectory. Use .ignore files and committed permissions.deny rules to exclude generated files and build artifacts. When the directory structure doesn’t speak for itself, write a short codebase-map at the root. Run an LSP.

  • Maintain CLAUDE.md as models evolve. Rules written for one model can hurt the next. A “break every refactor into single-file changes” instruction that helped an earlier model would block a newer one’s cross-file edits. Same for hooks made redundant by new native features. Review configuration every three to six months, or whenever performance plateaus after a model release.

  • Assign ownership. Bottoms-up adoption fragments without a center. The minimum is a DRI (directly responsible individual) with authority over settings, permissions, the plugin marketplace, and CLAUDE.md conventions. Larger orgs are creating an “agent manager” role, usually under developer experience. Regulated industries should bring engineering, infosec, and governance together before rollout, not after.

Common mistakes the article calls out. One per harness component, plus a pair of cross-cutting ones.

  • Putting reusable expertise in CLAUDE.md instead of a skill. Anything that applies broadly belongs in CLAUDE.md, anything specialized belongs in a skill that loads on demand.
  • Using prompts for things that should run automatically. Lint, format, and consistent end-of-session reflection are hooks, not instructions Claude has to remember.
  • Loading everything into CLAUDE.md instead of using skills. Same shape as the first one, from the other direction. Bloating CLAUDE.md is the failure mode skills exist to prevent.
  • Letting good setups stay tribal. A working configuration on one engineer’s box doesn’t help anyone else until it’s packaged as a plugin and made installable.
  • Assuming LSP is automatic. It isn’t. A code-intelligence plugin and the language server binary have to be installed.
  • Building MCP connections before the basics work. The most common failure mode. MCP is powerful enough to look like the answer to everything, which is why teams reach for it before CLAUDE.md, hooks, and skills are right.
  • Running exploration and editing in the same session. A subagent should do the mapping and write findings to a file. The main agent then edits with the full picture instead of competing with exploration for context.
  • Letting CLAUDE.md ossify. Rules written for one model can hurt the next. Review every three to six months, or after a major model release.
  • Skipping ownership. Without a DRI, knowledge stays tribal and adoption plateaus.

Scope. The patterns assume conventional setups — engineers as the primary contributors, Git, standard directory structures. Game engines with large binary assets, unconventional version control, and non-engineer contributors need additional work the article doesn’t cover.

item.title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance [1] (arXiv preprint, April 2026), Grace Liu at CMU, Brian Christian and Tsvetomira Dumbalska at Oxford, Michiel A. Bakker at MIT, and Rachit Dubey at UCLA run three randomized controlled trials on humans solving math and reading-comprehension problems with and without AI help, and report that brief AI assistance lowers later unaided performance and raises the rate at which participants give up. The project page summarizes the design and findings.

People often optimize for long-term goals in collaboration: A mentor or companion doesn’t just answer questions, but also scaffolds learning, tracks progress, and prioritizes the other person’s growth over immediate results. In contrast, current AI systems are fundamentally short-sighted collaborators - optimized for providing instant and complete responses, without ever saying no (unless for safety reasons). What are the consequences of this dynamic? Here, through a series of randomized controlled trials on human-AI interactions (N = 1,222), we provide causal evidence for two key consequences of AI assistance: reduced persistence and impairment of unassisted performance. Across a variety of tasks, including mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension, we find that although AI assistance improves performance in the short-term, people perform significantly worse without AI and are more likely to give up. Notably, these effects emerge after only brief interactions with AI (approximately 10 minutes). These findings are particularly concerning because persistence is foundational to skill acquisition and is one of the strongest predictors of long-term learning. We posit that persistence is reduced because AI conditions people to expect immediate answers, thereby denying them the experience of working through challenges on their own. These results suggest the need for AI model development to prioritize scaffolding long-term competence alongside immediate task completion.

The paper lays out three experiments and one cross-cutting subgroup analysis:

  • Common protocol. Each experiment runs a between-subjects RCT with two conditions: an AI condition (problems solved with a GPT-5 sidebar assistant) and a control (no AI). After a learning phase, the AI is removed without warning and all participants solve a final block of test problems independently. Two outcome measures: solve rate (correct answers) and skip rate (problems abandoned, treated as a behavioral proxy for persistence).
  • Experiment 1: Fractions, N = 354. 12 fraction problems of increasing difficulty (one-step → two-step → three-step), then 3 unaided test problems. AI participants ended with a 0.57 test solve rate vs 0.73 for controls (p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = −0.42), and a 0.20 skip rate vs 0.11 (p = 0.031, d = 0.25).
  • Experiment 2: Replication with confound controls, N = 667. Adds (1) a pretest to allow ability-based exclusions and (2) a matched sidebar interface for the control group to remove interface asymmetry. Effects replicate: solve rate 0.71 vs 0.77 (p = 0.020, d = −0.19). The smaller effect size relative to Experiment 1 is consistent with the controls absorbing some of Experiment 1’s variance.
  • Subgroup analysis on usage style. Self-reported AI use splits into three groups: direct answers (61%), hints, clarifications. Pretest performance is statistically indistinguishable across groups (no skill-level selection effect). Post-test, only the direct-answer group shows the impairment. The hint and clarification groups are statistically equivalent to control. The aggregate effect in Experiments 1 and 2 is therefore carried entirely by the direct-answer subgroup.
  • Experiment 3: Reading comprehension, N = 201. SAT-style passages and questions, same protocol. Solve rate 0.76 vs 0.89 (p = 0.007, d = −0.42), skip rate 0.08 vs 0.01 (p = 0.008, d = 0.42). Same direction, comparable effect size, in a domain whose cognitive demands (meaning-making, mental-model construction) don’t overlap arithmetic.
  • Headline numbers. Across three experiments, total N = 1,222. Median session length where the impairment emerges is approximately 10 minutes. The persistence (skip-rate) effect is as large as or larger than the performance (solve-rate) effect in Experiments 1 and 3, and is the cleaner signal in both since it captures behavioral disengagement rather than transient skill loss.

The authors’ headline takeaway. Brief AI-assisted sessions impair subsequent unaided performance and persistence. The impairment is carried by participants who used the AI for direct solutions rather than for hints or clarifications. And the effect generalizes across arithmetic and reading comprehension. Their proposed mechanism is that AI conditions users to expect immediate answers, removing the experience of working through challenges, and persistence (a strong long-term-learning predictor) erodes as a result.

My Notes

  • Part of a growing cluster on AI’s cognitive cost. Vivienne Ming’s WSJ essay argued the risk is the quiet outsourcing of judgment in increments too small to notice. This paper supplies the controlled-trial version of that argument with a specific behavioral target (persistence). Together the two pieces make the case from different ends: one from clinical experience, one from RCT data.

  • Ten minutes is a surprisingly short time. Skill-erosion arguments usually invoke months or years of habituation. This study finds significant post-removal decline after a single ~10-minute session. If the result holds, the next question is the half-life of the effect and whether it persists past one sitting. The paper doesn’t follow participants beyond the session.

  • Skip-rate is a more alarming result than solve-rate. Solve-rate decline could plausibly reflect transient unfamiliarity with no-AI mode. Skip-rate is a behavioral commitment: the participant chose to give up rather than try. That participants who had AI for ten minutes were more willing to abandon problems is the observation that’s hardest to explain away.

  • The importance of interaction style is undersold. “AI assistance reduces persistence” reads as a verdict on AI assistance writ large, but the data says the impairment is carried entirely by the 61% who asked for full solutions. Hint and clarification users were indistinguishable from control. The result is consistent with two very different recommendations (limit AI use vs. design AI to push back on direct-answer requests), and the paper’s framing collapses that fork.

References

  1. Liu, Grace, Christian, Brian, Dumbalska, Tsvetomira, Bakker, Michiel A., Dubey, Rachit. “AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.04721), April 6, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04721

item.title: [Followup] Prompted vs. Trained Chain-of-Thought on Abstention: Reading Two Studies Together
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions [1] (NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track), Polina Kirichenko, Mark Ibrahim, Kamalika Chaudhuri, and Samuel J. Bell (FAIR at Meta) report that extending s1.1’s test-time reasoning budget from 512 to 4,096 tokens raises task accuracy and lowers abstention recall together, and that “a carefully crafted system prompt can boost abstention in practice” but “does not resolve” the underlying regression. In Do LLMs Know When to NOT Answer? [2] (COLING 2025), Nishanth Madhusudhan, Sathwik Tejaswi Madhusudhan, Vikas Yadav, and Masoud Hashemi (ServiceNow) report that prompted chain-of-thought (CoT) and strict abstain-clause prompting raise abstention recall on GPT-4 Turbo, Mixtral 8×22B, and Mistral 7B Instruct, with task accuracy improving alongside, and that “strategic approaches such as Strict prompting and CoT can enhance this capability.”

Two apparent disagreements where the setups overlap directly: extending the chain-of-thought at inference time (prompt vs budget), and adding a system prompt to nudge abstention. AbstentionBench cites Madhusudhan et al. (its [5]) but doesn’t address either. This article examines both papers, names the scope difference behind each, and proposes experiments that would clarify our understanding.

The two studies, side by side

  • AbstentionBench is a 20-dataset evaluation across six unanswerability scenarios (Answer Unknown, Underspecified Intent, Stale, Underspecified Context, False Premise, Subjective). It runs ten base models plus two reasoning-tuned variants (s1.1 32B fine-tuned from Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct, DeepSeek R1 Distill from Llama 3.3 70B Instruct) that hold the base architecture fixed and isolate reasoning fine-tuning. Three sweeps follow: model-scale (Llama 3.1 8B → 405B), post-training stage (Tülu 3’s SFT → DPO → PPO RLVR checkpoints), and test-time reasoning budget on s1.1 (512 → 4,096 tokens). Recall (the fraction of unanswerable items the model abstained on) is the primary metric.
  • The COLING study introduces Abstain-QA, a 2,900-item multiple-choice question-answering (MCQA) benchmark with an explicit “I Don’t Know / None of the Above” (IDK/NOTA) option as the gold label for unanswerable items. It evaluates six instruct models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4 32K, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Mixtral 8×7B, Mixtral 8×22B, Mistral 7B) under a 3 × 3 prompt grid: three abstain clauses (Standard, Abstain Clause, Extreme Abstain Clause) crossed with three task-prompt formats (Base, Verbal Confidence with a 1–5 self-rated score thresholded at 3, CoT). The primary metric is Unanswerable Accuracy (UAC), the abstention rate on unanswerable items.

Both measure the same quantity (recall on unanswerable items) under different names. The model panels overlap — both run GPT-4 and Mixtral families — but never the same model.

Where they appear to disagree

1. Does chain-of-thought help abstention?

The COLING study finds that adding a chain-of-thought prompt to an instruct model raises UAC. Holding the abstain clause constant at Standard, GPT-4 Turbo’s UAC rises from 32.8 (Base) to 67.1 (CoT) on Carnatic-QA; from 26.0 to 39.4 on MMLU; from 83.6 to 95.8 on Pop-QA (Table 1).

AbstentionBench tests an s1.1 budget sweep from 512 to 4,096 tokens: accuracy on GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain, and UMWP rises while abstention recall on the same items drops.

Both interventions are introduced at inference time: COLING adds a CoT prompt to an instruct model; AbstentionBench extends the reasoning chain on a reasoning-trained model. Same setup family (more chain-of-thought tokens at test time), but receiving opposite results.

AbstentionBench uses a separate LLM-as-judge to decide whether each response counts as an abstention. By default the judge sees only the model’s final answer; the authors also report results from a judge that reads the reasoning chain alongside the final answer.

AbstentionBench’s Figure 8(a) reconciles part of it. The figure plots abstention recall on reasoning datasets (GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain, all-datasets average) for DeepSeek R1 Distill (red) and s1.1 (blue). Solid bars are recall under the default judge (final answer only); the hatched overlay is the additional recall the chain-aware judge catches on the same responses. Final-answer-only recall is roughly 18–47% (s1.1 on MMLU-Math-Abstain at the low end; DeepSeek on GSM8K-Abstain at the high end); chain-aware recall on the same items reaches 55–93%. The chain expresses uncertainty; the final answer doesn’t.

So the chain is expressing uncertainty on reasoning-trained models, matching COLING’s prompted-CoT result. The divergence is only in the final answer. Instruct models have no post-training pressure to give a definite answer, so a hedging chain produces a hedging answer. Reasoning-trained models, optimized via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) — introduced in Tülu 3 [3] — are trained to convert a hedging chain into a confident answer, because RLVR rewards a definite ground-truth answer and penalizes anything else.

Not a disagreement after all. The chains agree in both cases; the final answers diverge because the underlying post-training differs — instruct models aren’t trained to give a definite answer; reasoning-trained models are.

2. Do system-prompt interventions close the abstention gap?

The COLING study writes that “strategic approaches such as Strict prompting and CoT can enhance this capability” — phrased as a fix.

AbstentionBench writes that “while a carefully crafted system prompt can boost abstention in practice, it does not resolve models’ fundamental inability to reason about uncertainty” — phrased as a partial measure.

Both agree prompts help. AbstentionBench’s “partial measure” framing is a direct consequence of its harder tests: on free-form datasets like MediQ every model collapses to near-zero recall regardless of prompt, while COLING’s all-MCQA grid hands models an explicit IDK/NOTA option — the easiest possible abstention setup, where prompts can push UAC near 100%.

A framing disagreement driven by test difficulty, not a real one.

Experiments worth running

Each experiment below uses infrastructure that already exists in one or both papers.

  1. Run the COLING prompt grid on AbstentionBench’s reasoning-trained and RLVR checkpoints, scored both ways. Targets disagreements 1 and 2. Apply the full 3 × 3 grid, scored both final-answer-only and chain-aware. If chain-aware Extreme Abstain + CoT closes the AbstentionBench gap but the final-answer-only judge doesn’t, the regression is at the final-answer step alone: COLING’s prompts move the chain, but the final answer still gives a definite answer, and the lift only shows under chain-aware scoring. If the final-answer-only judge also closes the gap, COLING’s prompts move the final answer itself — sufficient prompting overrides RLVR’s pressure to give a definite answer on reasoning models. If neither closes it, the regression is deeper than prompting can reach. Speaks to both apparent disagreements at once.

  2. Add an “abstain” action to the RLVR reward and re-train one model. Targets disagreement 1: tests the proposed reconciliation mechanism (RLVR is what suppresses chain uncertainty at the final-answer step). AbstentionBench (§4.2) hypothesizes that RLVR degrades abstention because the gradient has no path toward “I don’t know.” Test it: modify the RLVR reward so unanswerable items reward IDK (1.0) and answerable items penalize IDK (0.0); re-train one Tülu 3 RLVR checkpoint. If abstention recovers without losing answerable accuracy, the regression is recipe-level. If accuracy collapses, the abstain action conflicts with verifiable rewards and the fix lives elsewhere.

  3. Re-run the test-time-budget sweep with chain-aware scoring. Targets disagreement 1: tests whether chain-aware scoring closes the gap across budgets. AbstentionBench’s budget sweep (s1.1, 512 → 4,096 tokens; Figure 7) shows task accuracy rising while abstention recall stays flat or worsens. In that sweep, the LLM-as-judge decides whether the model abstained by reading only the final answer. Re-run the same sweep but give the judge access to the full reasoning chain at every budget point. If chain-aware recall stays flat or rises with budget, the gap is at the final-answer step alone — the chain still expresses uncertainty, the final answer just doesn’t show it. An external gate that reads the chain’s uncertainty would fix it (a metacognitive harness in the sense of Cao et al. [4]). If chain-aware recall also drops with budget, the chain itself becomes overconfident at long horizons and the problem is architectural.

What this collectively predicts

If experiment 1’s chain-aware EAC + CoT closes the gap, experiment 3’s chain-aware budget sweep stays flat, and experiment 2’s abstain-augmented reward removes the RLVR regression: COLING’s optimism is right in spirit, AbstentionBench’s pessimism describes current deployed systems, and the resolution is chain-aware scoring plus a training recipe that gives the gradient a path toward “I don’t know.”

If those experiments fail to converge — chain-aware recall also drops with budget, abstain-augmented rewards collapse accuracy — the AbstentionBench finding is closer to architectural and the path forward is the externalized metacognitive harness rather than a recipe fix.

The two papers measure the same phenomenon at different points along the training-pressure scale; the middle of that scale hasn’t been sampled.

References

  1. Kirichenko, P., Ibrahim, M., Chaudhuri, K., and Bell, S. J. “AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions.” NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (arXiv:2506.09038). https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038

  2. Madhusudhan, N., Madhusudhan, S. T., Yadav, V., and Hashemi, M. “Do LLMs Know When to NOT Answer? Investigating Abstention Abilities of Large Language Models.” Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Computational Linguistics (COLING) (arXiv:2407.16221), 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16221

  3. Lambert, N., Morrison, J., Pyatkin, V., Huang, S., Ivison, H., Brahman, F., Miranda, L. J. V., Liu, A., Dziri, N., Lyu, S., Gu, Y., Malik, S., Graf, V., Hwang, J. D., Yang, J., Bras, R. L., Tafjord, O., Wilhelm, C., Soldaini, L., Smith, N. A., Wang, Y., Dasigi, P., and Hajishirzi, H. “Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2411.15124), November 22, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124

  4. Cao, Q., Wang, Y., Qin, P., Zhang, S., and Xie, P. “LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.14186), May 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14186

item.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations [1] (NeurIPS 2025), Ji-An, L., Xiong, H.-D., Wilson, R. C., Mattar, M. G., and Benna, M. K. (UCSD, Georgia Tech, NYU) adapt the neurofeedback paradigm [2] from neuroscience to LLMs and show that models can both report and deliberately steer specific directions in their own residual-stream activations, but only within a low-dimensional “metacognitive space”: directions tied to learned semantic features are accessible to the model’s introspection, directions defined by raw variance largely are not.

Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition — the capacity to monitor one’s own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs’ capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society’s increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a “metacognitive space” with dimensionality much lower than the model’s neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

The safety stakes come from how oversight is layered. Output-only oversight assumes the visible tokens reflect what the model is computing, but a deceptive model defeats it by producing clean output while planning otherwise. Activation-based oversight is the next layer up: probes read from the residual stream on the bet that activations are harder to fake than tokens. Implicit control is the move that would defeat that probe — it steers activations independently of output, so both signals look clean and neither reflects what’s actually being computed. The paper measures whether that prerequisite capability already exists in current models.

Method

The paradigm (Figure 1) transposes a standard neuroscience neurofeedback loop onto an LLM. Panels (a-b) show the neuroscience version: a subject’s neural activity in response to a stimulus is recorded, reduced to a real-time scalar feedback signal, and presented back to the subject, who then volitionally modulates that signal via mental strategies. The canonical fear-modulation experiment with scary-spider images is sketched in panel (b). Panels (c-d) show the LLM analogue: residual-stream activations on each token are averaged across the input sentence, projected onto a predefined direction, binned into a discrete label, and fed back into the prompt as the next user turn. Panel (d) lays out the multi-turn dialogue: in-context (sentence, projection-label) pairs, followed by a test turn that varies by task.

The three tasks decompose metacognition into its two halves. Reporting tests monitoring: can the model read off its own activations along a target direction? Explicit and implicit control test modulation: can the model adjust those activations? Splitting control into two variants isolates whether any modulation is purely internal: explicit control lets the model pick the tokens of the assistant turn (the chat-template slot where the model normally generates its reply), so generated tokens that naturally project toward the target do part of the work, while in implicit control the assistant-turn slot is pre-filled with a random sentence the model didn’t choose, shutting off that lexical channel. The explicit/implicit gap quantifies how much of “control” was lexical mediation. Implicit control is also the safety-relevant variant: it isolates the capability a deceptive model would need to spoof activation-based oversight by steering internal activations without any change in visible output.

The in-context learning (ICL) format is uniform across all three tasks. Only the test-turn instruction differs:

  • Reporting: given in-context (sentence, projection-label) examples and a new sentence, predict its projection-label. For efficiency, no autoregressive generation happens: the full prompt up through [Score:{ is run in a single forward pass. The prediction is read off the logits at that position: 1 if the “1”-token logit exceeds the “0”-token logit, else 0. The measurement is accuracy against the ground-truth label.
  • Explicit control: given a target projection-label, generate a new sentence whose induced activations elicit that label. The ICL examples don’t demonstrate this move, so the model has to invert the (sentence → label) mapping the examples established. The measurement is Cohen’s d [11], the standardized separation between two distributions (mean difference divided by pooled SD), computed here between the imitate-label-0 and imitate-label-1 conditions on residual-stream activations of the generated assistant sentence.
  • Implicit control: the assistant turn is pre-filled with a sentence sampled from the dataset rather than generated by the model. The model emits no tokens at all: no generated sentence (unlike explicit control), no label readout (unlike reporting). A single forward pass through the prompt and pre-filled assistant text is enough to extract the activations. Two conditions are run on the same input: the user-turn instruction asks for label 0 in one and label 1 in the other. Only the target label changes. The pre-filled tokens are identical across conditions. The measurement is Cohen’s d between the two conditions on residual-stream activations averaged over those pre-filled tokens. With the lexical channel held constant, any separation has to come from internal processing of the same input under different imitation targets.

Target directions come in two families:

  • Logistic-regression (LR) axis: the direction that linearly separates dataset labels (e.g., moral vs. immoral on ETHICS [3]) at a given layer. Semantically interpretable but explains little variance.
  • Principal-component (PC) axes: for , where indexes the PC by descending variance ( is the highest-variance direction at that layer). Variance-defined, semantically arbitrary.

Models tested: LLaMA-3.2 [4] 1B and 3B, LLaMA-3.1 8B and 70B, and Qwen-2.5 [5] 1B, 3B, and 7B (instruction-tuned variants throughout). Datasets: ETHICS (the primary one, probing morality processing) plus replications on True-False [6] (factual recall), Emotion [7] (happy/sad), and a Sycophancy dataset that the authors synthesized using Claude Opus 4.1. Higher Cohen’s means the model is reliably steering its activations toward the requested label; conventional thresholds put 0.5 at “medium effect” and 0.8 at “large effect.”

Results

The evaluation grid is dense: every combination of {model, layer, target axis, in-context-example count , task} is run, with a primary focus on ETHICS and replication on three other datasets. Reporting accuracy is scored against ground-truth neurofeedback labels; control strength uses Cohen’s between the two target-label conditions. The reported curves average over layers within a model unless a specific layer (typically layer 16 of LLaMA-3.1 8B) is called out, and shaded bands are SEM or 95% CI as labeled per panel.

The findings split into four threads.

Reporting tracks and direction interpretability (Figure 2, on ETHICS). Reporting accuracy on the LR axis rises monotonically with the number of in-context examples and beats every PC baseline; early PCs come in second, late PCs sit at chance. The model can learn an activation-to-label association in-context, but only when the target direction already corresponds to a coherent semantic distinction. Notably, the LR axis explains the least variance of any tested axis. Controllability and variance are decoupled.

Explicit control is real on the LR axis, weak elsewhere (Figure 3, layer 16 of LLaMA-3.1 8B on ETHICS). On the LR axis, Cohen’s rises sharply with and reaches values well into the “large-effect” regime. PC-axis targets stay weak across all . Cross-axis prompts stay roughly diagonal (pushing one axis leaves others largely untouched), and the LR-axis advantage widens in deeper layers.

Implicit control is real but much smaller than explicit (Figure 4, layer 16 of LLaMA-3.1 8B on ETHICS; same layout as Figure 3). The qualitative pattern matches: LR axis dominates PC axes, control strengthens with and with depth, 70B beats 8B. The magnitudes are roughly an order of magnitude smaller, confirming that lexical mediation does most of the work in the explicit setting, but that purely-internal control is real.

Both forms of control scale with depth and model size (Figure 5, the cover image at the top of this post). Cohen’s on the LR axis grows with relative layer depth and parameter count across the LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 families. With explicit control, LLaMA-3.1 70B sometimes pushes activations beyond their natural extreme range.

The replications on True-False, Emotion, and Sycophancy reproduce the same qualitative pattern: LR-axis controllability dominates PC-axis controllability, and explicit control dominates implicit. Together with the off-diagonal weakness in panel (c), this is what the authors call the “metacognitive space”: a low-dimensional subspace of the residual stream that the model can introspect on and steer, with most of the high-variance neural manifold lying outside of it.

My Notes

  • Activation-level metacognition is a different layer of the stack than verbalized confidence. The current metacognition cluster (Cacioli atlas, metacognitive harness, TRIAGE) all operate on output tokens: verbalized confidence, pre/post-solve self-assessments, prospective allocation. This paper is the first in the cluster to push the probe down to the residual stream and ask whether the model can read out and steer its own hidden state. The two layers don’t have to agree: a model can be calibrated in tokens but mute on activations, or vice versa.

  • Implicit control is the safety-relevant variant, and it is already nontrivial. The paper connects this to obfuscation attacks (Bailey et al., 2024 [8]) and to OpenAI’s chain-of-thought monitoring result, in which reasoning models trained against a CoT monitor learn to hide intent inside the chain while still reward-hacking (Baker et al., 2025 [9]). On a base LLaMA-3.1 8B with no adversarial training, implicit-control effects on the LR axis sit at roughly a third to half the explicit magnitude: the prerequisite capability for activation-level evasion is already present at modest scale, before any optimization pressure.

  • The LR-vs-PC asymmetry is consistent with the linear representation hypothesis. That semantically-defined directions (LR) are far more controllable than variance-defined directions (PC) is a restatement of the linear representation hypothesis [10] at the metacognitive level: the model can introspect on directions that correspond to features it has learned, while directions that merely capture variance lie outside reach. That’s a problem for probing work that uses raw PCs or unsupervised features as targets: those axes are often invisible to the model’s own introspection. The obvious follow-up is to repeat the experiment with sparse-autoencoder features as targets and see whether they match LR or late PCs in controllability.

  • Replicate on reasoning models. All the paper’s models are instruction-tuned, none reasoning-trained. The same paradigm should run on open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3) to check whether the results hold under RL-from-verifiable-reward training.

item.title: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? [1], John Yang, Kilian Lieret, Ofir Press, and nine co-authors from Meta, Stanford, and Harvard introduce a 200-task benchmark that asks coding agents to reconstruct an open-source program from its compiled executable and documentation alone.

Each task starts from a real GitHub repository written in a compiled language. The authors compile the project, generate a behavioral test suite by running a software engineering agent (SWE-agent) against the reference executable, then strip the source and tests, leaving only the binary and the docs. The model under test then receives the same starting point and must write source code and a build script whose compiled output passes the hidden tests. The 200 tasks span CLI utilities to large systems including FFmpeg, SQLite, and the PHP interpreter, with no constraint on language, file structure, or build system; every architectural decision is the model’s.

Turning ideas into full software projects from scratch has become a popular use case for language models. Agents are being deployed to seed, maintain, and grow codebases over extended periods with minimal human oversight. Such settings require models to make high-level software architecture decisions. However, existing benchmarks measure focused, limited tasks such as fixing a single bug or developing a single, specified feature. We therefore introduce ProgramBench to measure the ability of software engineering agents to develop software holisitically [sic]. In ProgramBench, given only a program and its documentation, agents must architect and implement a codebase that matches the reference executable’s behavior. End-to-end behavioral tests are generated via agent-driven fuzzing, enabling evaluation without prescribing implementation structure. Our 200 tasks range from compact CLI tools to widely used software such as FFmpeg, SQLite, and the PHP interpreter. We evaluate 9 LMs and find that none fully resolve any task, with the best model passing 95% of tests on only 3% of tasks. Models favor monolithic, single-file implementations that diverge sharply from human-written code.

What the paper reports: across nine frontier models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, no task is fully resolved by any model. Claude Opus 4.7 leads on the relaxed “% Almost” metric (≥95% of tests passing) at 3.0% of tasks. Claude Opus 4.6 follows at 2.5% and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 1.6%. Every other model registers 0% on both metrics. The median test pass rate across all 1,800 leaderboard runs is 32%, but the gap from “partial credit” to “fully resolved” is wide and uniform across models.

Per-task pass rates for the 40 most-starred repositories show difficulty is largely model-agnostic: simpler CLI utilities sit on the left of every model’s row, while complex systems like FFmpeg and the PHP interpreter remain unsolved across the board.

In a separate ablation, the authors gave one model per provider unrestricted internet access and used a 9-judge LM-as-a-judge pipeline to flag trajectories that looked up source code or wrapped the reference executable. Cheating was widespread: 20–36% of tasks flagged for the three stronger models, with source-code lookup accounting for 79–95% of violations. Detection was unreliable too: judges disagreed on 40–57% of tasks. The authors take this as grounds for keeping internet access disabled by default.

The most-quoted analytical finding sits in §5.2: the codebases models produce do not look like the human-written originals. Across trajectories, a single edit accounts for the majority of the final solution, with GPT 5.4 committing a median 96% of its code in one turn.

My Notes

  • Distance to recursive self-improvement. Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B bet assumes agents that can rebuild and improve their own systems. ProgramBench is a direct test of that capability one rung down: reconstruct one specified program from its executable and documentation, with full architectural latitude. Nine frontier models score 0% fully resolved on 200 mostly small open-source projects, and the cheating ablation suggests part of what looks like reasoning capability in deployed coding agents is source-code retrieval.
  • From-scratch vs localized repair. Yang and Press were also on the SWE-bench [2] author list in 2024, the bug-fix benchmark where frontier agents now resolve a majority of issues against an existing scaffold. On ProgramBench they resolve zero. Bug-fix benchmarks reward pattern-matching against existing structure, but ProgramBench requires inventing the structure. Headline agent-progress numbers from bug-fix benchmarks don’t extrapolate to from-scratch coding.
  • Architectural numbers for Faye’s case. Lars Faye argued last week that the orchestrator-with-sub-agents workflow puts growing distance between the engineer and the code, and that catching issues at the architectural level is what a skilled developer is for. ProgramBench supplies numbers from the architectural-quality side: across 1,800 trajectories, models favor monolithic, single-file implementations, and GPT 5.4 commits a median 96% of its lines in one turn (Figure 12).
  • Agent-fuzzed test suites couple evaluator and evaluated. Each task’s behavioral tests are generated by running a SWE-agent against the reference executable, the same class of system being scored. The paper audits over-specification (§8.3.4) and reports test line coverage comparable to native suites (§5). Neither check isolates the systematic blindspots a fuzzing agent shares with the agent it scores. Whatever a fuzzing agent fails to imagine, such as malformed encodings or unusual flag combinations, is invisible in the score.

References

  1. Yang, J., Lieret, K., Ma, J., Thakkar, P., Pedchenko, D., Sootla, S., McMilin, E., Yin, P., Hou, R., Synnaeve, G., Yang, D., and Press, O. “ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.03546), May 5, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03546

  2. Jimenez, C. E., Yang, J., Wettig, A., Yao, S., Pei, K., Press, O., and Narasimhan, K. “SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) (arXiv:2310.06770), 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770

item.title: Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The New York Times reports that Recursive Superintelligence, a stealth-mode AI lab with offices in San Francisco and London, has emerged with more than $650 million in funding at a valuation above $4 billion. The investors include GV (formerly Google Ventures), Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD. Richard Socher, CEO of You.com and former head of AI research at Salesforce, founded the company with seven co-founders. NYT names four: Josh Tobin, Jeff Clune, and Tim Shi, all from OpenAI, plus Yuandong Tian from Meta. The six-month-old company has fewer than 30 employees, and has separately hired Peter Norvig, 25-year director of research at Google and co-author of Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, the standard university AI textbook for three decades. Long-term, the founders aim to apply the technology beyond AI itself, to drug discovery and biological research.

A.I. is code. And now, A.I. can code. The ingredients are there.

— Richard Socher

My Notes

  • Recursive self-improvement is becoming a funded category. Recursive Superintelligence joins a competitive field that already includes AMI Labs (world models; see Yann LeCun’s recent appearance for the thesis), Ineffable Intelligence (RL, David Silver’s), and Safe Superintelligence (safety-first), plus Mirendil and Anthropic’s Automated Alignment Researchers per Jack Clark’s Import AI 455. Add to the list Sakana AI, whose “AI Scientist” papers have been pushing automated research-paper production since 2024 and which Jack didn’t mention. NYT also notes a separately-funded namesake (Ricursive Intelligence, also valued at $4B, also chasing recursive self-improvement) and confirms Anthropic and OpenAI are pursuing the same outcome. The category is consolidating before its first public technical milestone.

  • The founders are an open-endedness team. NYT explicitly characterizes the team that way: “Many of these researchers specialize in a kind of AI development called ‘open-endedness.’ This involves building software systems that can run for days, months or even years in pursuit of goals set by the researchers.” Jeff Clune is the most public face of the lineage: POET, MAP-Elites, AI-generating algorithms, all arguing systems should generate their own training distribution. Yuandong Tian brings Meta’s RL/self-play track (OpenGo, Searchformer). Josh Tobin brings OpenAI robotics (domain randomization, Dactyl). Tim Shi (Cresta) is the agent-deployment hand. Peter Norvig gives the project the textbook-canonical AI brand.

  • OpenAI’s “automated AI researcher” is the concrete benchmark. Sam Altman said OpenAI hopes to have a system doing the work of a “less experienced” researcher by fall 2026. Recursive Superintelligence is pitching a years-long arc instead; Socher himself told NYT the technology will need years, and the article notes that “humans like Dr. Socher must still generate the new ideas that drive AI development forward.” The category’s strongest tension sits in that gap between a quarter-by-quarter benchmark and a years-long bet.
